summary.text: Writing the zeta values as Dirichlet series, the proof truncates \(\sum k^{-n}\) after \(k=10\) and \(\sum k^{-2n}\) after \(k=3\), bounding the tails by telescoping estimates as \(O(11^{-n})\). A finite algebraic expansion then cancels the desired low-base terms, leaving only monomials whose combined bases are at least \(11\); division by the remaining denominator is harmless because it is bounded below by \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
t(n)=\frac{\zeta(2n)}{\zeta(n)^2}\qquad(n\ge 2).
\]
We prove that
\[
\frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}
 =2^{-n}+3^{-n}+5^{-n}+7^{-n}+O(11^{-n}).
\]
All asymptotic statements below are for positive integers \(n\to\infty\). Since changing finitely many values does not affect a big-O statement, it is enough throughout to work with \(n\ge2\).

First we establish a tail estimate that will be used twice.

### 1. A general estimate for Dirichlet-series tails

For integers \(m\ge2\),
\[
\frac1{m^2}\le \frac1{m-1}-\frac1m.
\]
Indeed, the expression on the right is \(1/(m(m-1))\), and \(m(m-1)\le m^2\).

Let \(K\ge2\) and \(n\ge2\). For every \(k\ge0\), factor
\[
(k+K)^{-n}=(k+K)^{-2}(k+K)^{-(n-2)}.
\]
Because \(k+K\ge K\), this gives
\[
(k+K)^{-n}\le (k+K)^{-2}K^{-(n-2)}.
\]
Applying the preceding inequality to \(m=k+K\), summing, and using telescoping, we obtain for every \(N\ge0\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(k+K)^{-n}
&\le K^{-(n-2)}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}
 \left(\frac1{k+K-1}-\frac1{k+K}\right)\\
&=K^{-(n-2)}\left(\frac1{K-1}-\frac1{N+K-1}\right)\\
&\le \frac1{K-1}K^{-(n-2)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Letting \(N\to\infty\),
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+K)^{-n}
 \le \frac1{K-1}K^{-(n-2)}.}
\tag{1}
\]
In particular, if \(K\ge11\), the right side is \(O(11^{-n})\): explicitly,
\[
\frac1{K-1}K^{-(n-2)}
\le \frac{K^2}{K-1}\,11^{-n},
\]
since \(K^{-n}\le11^{-n}\). We shall only need the case \(K=11\).

We will also repeatedly use the following elementary observation. If \(v\ge11\), then
\[
v^{-n}\le11^{-n},
\]
so \(v^{-n}=O(11^{-n})\). More generally, for nonnegative integers \(p,q,r,s\),
\[
(2^{-n})^p(3^{-n})^q(5^{-n})^r(7^{-n})^s
 =\bigl(2^p3^q5^r7^s\bigr)^{-n}.
\tag{2}
\]
Thus this monomial is \(O(11^{-n})\) whenever
\(2^p3^q5^r7^s\ge11\). Multiplication by a fixed coefficient and addition of finitely many such monomials preserve the same big-O estimate.

### 2. Truncating the two zeta values

For an integer \(n>1\), the absolutely convergent Dirichlet series gives
\[
\zeta(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-n}.
\]
Introduce the abbreviations
\[
a=2^{-n},\qquad b=3^{-n},\qquad d=5^{-n},\qquad f=7^{-n}.
\]
Then
\[
a^2=4^{-n},\quad ab=6^{-n},\quad a^3=8^{-n},
\quad b^2=9^{-n},\quad ad=10^{-n}.
\]
Define
\[
P_0=a+b+a^2+d+ab+f+a^3+b^2+ad
     =\sum_{m=2}^{10}m^{-n}
\]
and
\[
E_1=\sum_{m=11}^{\infty}m^{-n}.
\]
Thus
\[
Z_1:=\zeta(n)=1+P_0+E_1.
\tag{3}
\]
Taking \(K=11\) in (1),
\[
0\le E_1\le \frac1{10}11^{-(n-2)}
 =\frac{121}{10}\,11^{-n},
\]
so
\[
E_1=O(11^{-n}).
\tag{4}
\]

Similarly, put
\[
Q_0=a^2+b^2=4^{-n}+9^{-n}

a
\]
(the isolated “a” here is not intended; equivalently simply take \(Q_0=a^2+b^2\)) and
\[
E_2=\sum_{m=4}^{\infty}m^{-2n}.
\]
Then
\[
Z_2:=\zeta(2n)=1+Q_0+E_2,
\tag{5}
\]
because the terms for \(m=2,3\) are \(4^{-n}\) and \(9^{-n}\).
Applying (1) with exponent \(2n\) and \(K=4\),
\[
0\le E_2\le \frac13\,4^{-(2n-2)}
 =\frac{16}{3}\,16^{-n}.
\]
Since \(16^{-n}\le11^{-n}\), it follows that
\[
E_2=O(11^{-n}).
\tag{6}
\]

Finally define the proposed main term
\[
P=a+b+d+f=2^{-n}+3^{-n}+5^{-n}+7^{-n}.
\tag{7}
\]
The quantities \(P_0\) and \(P\) are bounded as \(n\to\infty\), since each is a fixed finite sum of terms \(k^{-n}\le1\).

### 3. Cancellation of every term whose exponential base is below 11

The key finite algebraic assertion is
\[
N_0:=(1+P_0)^2-(1+Q_0)
-P\bigl((1+P_0)^2+(1+Q_0)\bigr)
=O(11^{-n}).
\tag{8}
\]
We now verify this assertion completely.

Expand it as
\[
N_0=(2P_0-Q_0-2P)+P_0^2-2PP_0-PQ_0-PP_0^2.
\tag{9}
\]
Every term in this expression is a fixed integer multiple of a monomial in \(a,b,d,f\). By (2), any monomial whose associated base is at least \(11\) is already \(O(11^{-n})\). It therefore remains only to calculate the monomials of base less than \(11\).

The summands of \(P_0\), together with their bases, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
\text{monomial}&a&b&a^2&d&ab&f&a^3&b^2&ad\\
\hline
\text{base}&2&3&4&5&6&7&8&9&10.
\end{array}
\]
Consequently the low-base part of the linear expression
\(2P_0-Q_0-2P\) is
\[
a^2+2ab+2a^3+b^2+2ad.
\tag{10}
\]
Indeed, the terms \(a,b,d,f\) cancel against \(2P\), while subtracting
\(Q_0=a^2+b^2\) changes the coefficients of \(a^2,b^2\) from \(2\) to \(1\).

For \(P_0^2\), a product can have base below \(11\) only in the following cases:
\[
2\cdot2=4,\quad 2\cdot3=6,\quad 2\cdot4=8,
\quad 3\cdot3=9,\quad 2\cdot5=10.
\]
The unequal pairs occur in both orders. Hence the low-base part of \(P_0^2\) is
\[
a^2+2ab+2a^3+b^2+2ad.
\tag{11}
\]

For \(-2PP_0\), the same five products are possible, but now the first factor must be one of \(a,b,d,f\). The product \(a\cdot b\) occurs both as \(a\) from \(P\) times \(b\) from \(P_0\), and as \(b\) from \(P\) times \(a\) from \(P_0\); likewise for \(ad\). The resulting low-base part is therefore
\[
-2a^2-4ab-2a^3-2b^2-4ad.
\tag{12}
\]

For \(-PQ_0\), where \(Q_0=a^2+b^2\), the only product of base below \(11\) is
\(a\cdot a^2=a^3\), of base \(8\). Thus its low-base part is
\[
-a^3.
\tag{13}
\]

Finally, the smallest-base monomial in \(P_0^2\) is \(a^2\), of base \(4\). In \(-PP_0^2\), multiplying this by \(a\), of base \(2\), gives \(-a^3\), of base \(8\). Every other possibility has base at least \(12\): either the factor from \(P\) has base at least \(3\), or the monomial from \(P_0^2\) has base at least \(6\). Therefore the low-base part of \(-PP_0^2\) is
\[
-a^3.
\tag{14}
\]

Adding (10)–(14), the coefficients cancel one by one:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
& a^2&ab&a^3&b^2&ad\\ \hline
(10)&1&2&2&1&2\\
(11)&1&2&2&1&2\\
(12)&-2&-4&-2&-2&-4\\
(13)&0&0&-1&0&0\\
(14)&0&0&-1&0&0\\ \hline
\text{total}&0&0&0&0&0.
\end{array}
\]
Thus every monomial of base below \(11\) vanishes. All remaining monomials have base at least \(11\), and there are only finitely many of them. By (2), their sum is \(O(11^{-n})\). This proves (8).

### 4. Restoring the tails

Consider the numerator obtained after subtracting \(P\) from the desired fraction:
\[
N:=Z_1^2-Z_2-P(Z_1^2+Z_2).
\tag{15}
\]
Substitute (3) and (5). Direct expansion, grouping first the expression with both tails set equal to zero, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
N={}&N_0
+E_1\bigl(2+2P_0-2P-2PP_0\bigr)\\
&+E_1^2(1-P)+E_2(-1-P).
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
\]
This identity follows simply by expanding
\((1+P_0+E_1)^2\) and collecting the constant, linear, and quadratic terms in \(E_1\), as well as the linear term in \(E_2\).

We already know from (8) that \(N_0=O(11^{-n})\). The coefficient
\[
2+2P_0-2P-2PP_0
\]
is bounded because \(P_0\) and \(P\) are bounded. Hence (4) shows that the second term in (16) is \(O(11^{-n})\).

Also, (4) implies that \(E_1\) is bounded; consequently
\(E_1^2=E_1\cdot E_1=O(11^{-n})\). Since \(1-P\) is bounded, the third term is \(O(11^{-n})\). Finally, \(-1-P\) is bounded, so (6) shows that the fourth term is \(O(11^{-n})\). We conclude from (16) that
\[
N=O(11^{-n}).
\tag{17}
\]

### 5. Division by the denominator and identification with \(t(n)\)

Every term in the Dirichlet series for \(Z_1=\zeta(n)\) and
\(Z_2=\zeta(2n)\) is nonnegative, and the term with index \(1\) equals \(1\). Therefore
\[
Z_1\ge1,\qquad Z_2\ge1.
\]
In particular,
\[
D:=Z_1^2+Z_2\ge1
\tag{18}
\]
(in fact \(D\ge2\)). Thus division by \(D\) cannot enlarge absolute values:
\[
\left|\frac{N}{D}\right|\le |N|.
\]
Combining this with (17),
\[
\frac{Z_1^2-Z_2-P(Z_1^2+Z_2)}{Z_1^2+Z_2}
=O(11^{-n}).
\tag{19}
\]
Since the denominator is nonzero, the left side is
\[
\frac{Z_1^2-Z_2}{Z_1^2+Z_2}-P.
\tag{20}
\]

For \(n\ge2\), the real Dirichlet-series identities above say exactly that
\(Z_1=\zeta(n)\) and \(Z_2=\zeta(2n)\). Therefore
\[
t(n)=\frac{Z_2}{Z_1^2}.
\]
As \(Z_1\ne0\), elementary division gives
\[
\frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}
=\frac{1-Z_2/Z_1^2}{1+Z_2/Z_1^2}
=\frac{Z_1^2-Z_2}{Z_1^2+Z_2}.
\tag{21}
\]
Using (7), (19), (20), and (21), we finally obtain
\[
\frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}
-\left(2^{-n}+3^{-n}+5^{-n}+7^{-n}\right)
=O(11^{-n}).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\frac{1-t(n)}{1+t(n)}
=\frac1{2^n}+\frac1{3^n}+\frac1{5^n}+\frac1{7^n}
+O\!\left(\frac1{11^n}\right).}
\]
This is the claimed asymptotic formula.
